resources.string: Simplified front projection and load paths. The moving markers show direction, not the speed or size of forces in a person.
The sacrum meets the two hip bones at the sacroiliac joints behind. The pubic symphysis joins both hip bones in front; the hip sockets face outward to meet the femurs.
Follow the paths to both hips
In supported standing, load from above reaches the sacrum and is transmitted through the pelvic ring toward both hip joints and the femurs.
The diagram widens the path toward the side taking more support. Actual hip contact forces also depend on muscle action and posture, which this diagram leaves out.
The example moves the applied load back toward the center. The drawing compares how support changes without implying that the ring opens or the bones separate.
This triangular bone connects the lower spine to the two sides of the pelvic ring.
The joint between the sacrum and ilium helps carry load from the spine into the hip bone.
The femoral head sits in this socket at the side of the hip bone.
Fibrocartilage connects the right and left pubic bones at the front of the ring.
How subcutaneous tissue cushions a load
Illustrated tissue deformation. The amount and speed of motion are exaggerated and do not represent measured tissue behavior.
Below the epidermis and dermis are fat lobules separated by connective-tissue septa. Deeper fascia separates the illustrated layer from muscle.
The surface indents. The fat lobules and their surrounding connective tissue change shape together while the deep boundary moves less in this example.
The layer changes its shape over a region rather than at a single point. Lines mark illustrative paths through the tissue, not an exact map of pressure.
The dashed line marks the original surface. This simplified reversible example returns toward that shape once the load is removed.
Clusters of fat-storing cells are arranged in groups within the subcutaneous layer.
Fibrous partitions divide adjacent fat lobules and connect layers of tissue.
A deeper connective-tissue boundary overlies the muscle shown here.
Mechanical response of human adipose tissue
A rigid weightless beam on two supports. This demonstrates static balance, not hip joint forces, walking, or personal measurements.
A load applied to a beam with two upward supports. As the load moves right, the right arrow grows and the left shrinks.
An ideal, evenly loaded contact area. This compares average pressure, not local pressure peaks, tissue deformation, or injury.
Two pads carry the same force. The contact strip becomes darker where the average pressure is greater.
